reasons: The article states: "Find the 'Help me write' bar. It usually appears just below the subject line once you've typed some text." In Gmail, the 'Help me write' button (with a sparkle icon) is located at the bottom of the compose window, not below the subject line. This is a fabricated description of a UI element's placement.

The article claims: "If you don't see it, look for a small lightning-bolt icon, which you can click to expand the AI assistant." The 'Help me write' feature is initiated by clicking a button (typically with a sparkle icon) at the bottom of the compose window; there isn't a lightning-bolt icon used to 'expand' a hidden AI assistant from below the subject line as described.

The article provides a keyboard shortcut: "After typing a prompt, press Ctrl + Enter (Windows) or Cmd + Enter (Mac) to apply it faster." This shortcut is not a documented or functional method for applying AI refinements within Gmail's 'Help me write' feature; Ctrl/Cmd + Enter is typically used to send the email itself.

The metadata field "tool: SkillOpt" is inaccurate. While SkillOpt is a real Microsoft Research initiative, the article explicitly states, "Even though you can't use SkillOpt directly," confirming it is not a user-facing tool for the audience of this guide. The article instead teaches how to use other AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) to simulate SkillOpt principles, meaning SkillOpt is not the tool being demonstrated or used by the reader.

The article repeatedly references "Microsoft's SkillOpt initiative" as a real cutting-edge research project in AI skill acquisition. A search for "Microsoft SkillOpt" yields no public or official initiative, research paper, or product by this name from Microsoft. This appears to be an invented name for a research initiative falsely attributed to Microsoft.
The product 'Omnigent' by Databricks is invented. There is no official Databricks product or announcement by this name related to AI agents and contextual policies.
The URL 'https://www.databricks.com/blog/contextual-policies-omnigent-using-session-state-better-govern-ai-agents' is invented. The blog post described does not exist on the Databricks website.

The source URL provided, http://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/06/create-fully-native-and-editable-presentations-with-Gemini-in-Google-Slides.html, uses a future date (2026) for an alleged past or current announcement, making it an invented URL.

The article describes a workflow for AI image super-resolution, including UI elements like 'Image Tools', 'AI Enhancements', 'Super-Resolution' sections, 'Upload Image' buttons, and options to configure 'Upscale Factor' and 'Sharpening'. These features and UI elements are attributed to 'an AI image enhancement application'. However, the specified tool, ChatRTX, is a local large language model (LLM) chatbot and does not possess any image super-resolution capabilities or the described user interface for image processing.

The article claims that users can 'Continue as guest' or proceed without logging in to DeepSeek Chat. DeepSeek Chat (chat.deepseek.com) requires users to log in with a Google, GitHub, or email account and does not offer a guest or anonymous access option.

The article lists "Lanzos" as an AI model option within Upscayl's "Models" section. Lanzos resampling is a traditional image scaling algorithm, not an AI super-resolution model that users select in Upscayl's interface alongside models like Real-ESRGAN or Remacri.

The article repeatedly claims that Grok is available on Amazon Bedrock. As of now, Grok (from xAI) is not one of the foundation models offered by Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock provides access to models from Amazon, Anthropic, AI21 Labs, Cohere, Meta, Mistral AI, and Stability AI, but not Grok.

The article refers to a specific AI capability within Google Vids as "Gemini Omni." While Google Vids is a real product powered by Gemini, there is no publicly announced or recognized AI capability specifically *called* "Gemini Omni" associated with Google Vids or the broader Gemini suite. The phrasing suggests a specific, named feature that does not exist.

The article implies that Google Vids directly 'generates a video clip' with 'better realism and even improved text rendering (how clearly words appear within the video)' from a simple text prompt. While Google Vids is an AI-powered video creation app that uses text prompts to generate storyboards, drafts, and voiceovers, it primarily assists in assembling and creating videos using existing or stock media and AI-generated elements, rather than generating novel, realistic video footage with embedded text from scratch as a pure text-to-video model would. This misrepresents its core generative capabilities for visual content.
The article describes a "Preview" tab on the right side of the screen in Step 2. In ChatGPT's custom GPT builder interface, there is a "Preview" *panel* on the right, not a tab.

In Step 2, the article states "If it looks different: The two sections might be labelled 'Build' and 'Configure,' or simply 'Create' and 'Test.'" While 'Create' and 'Configure' are the actual tab labels, 'Build' and 'Test' are not alternative labels for the main tabs in the custom GPT builder UI.

The article instructs users to "Select the 'Generate' model" within the Cohere Playground. 'Generate' is not a specific model name available for selection in the Cohere Playground/Workbench UI. Users typically select models like 'Command' or 'Command-R' to perform text generation tasks, including classification.

The article describes a 'New Chat' button or similar UI element (e.g., 'square with a pen icon', 'plus (+) sign') that clears previous conversations and history within Grok. Grok's interface operates as a continuous chat, where new prompts are simply typed into the existing conversation thread, and there is no dedicated 'New Chat' button for clearing chat history or starting a fresh, isolated conversation in the manner described.

The guide states that pasting a news article's web address (URL) into Grok is 'even easier' and 'ideally' how one should provide content 'so Grok can access all the details'. However, the 'Common mistakes' section explicitly states, 'Grok can't read articles behind paywalls... unless you manually paste the text into the chat.' This contradiction and the general presentation of URL pasting as a universally reliable and preferred method for fetching *all* article details, including potentially paywalled content, overstates Grok's current capabilities and reliability for such a feature.

The article describes a specific 'continuous translation mode' for Siri, activated by saying 'Continue translating' or 'Keep translating' after an initial translation, allowing users to speak new phrases directly and have them automatically translated into the last chosen language without reactivating Siri each time. This specific interaction flow and feature has not been announced or demonstrated as a capability of Siri, even with the enhancements of Apple Intelligence. While Siri has an 'Interpreter Mode' for two-way conversations, the described one-way, continuous input mode with these commands is not a known feature.

UI element: The article claims 'Grok's interface works like a continuous conversation, so there isn't a specific "new chat" button to clear previous discussions.' This is incorrect; Grok does have a 'New Chat' button or similar functionality to start a fresh conversation and clear previous context.

Step 2 describes a 'New Chat' button or a 'square with a plus sign inside it' icon for Grok. Grok's interface within X typically operates as a continuous chat where users type new queries into the same window, and it does not usually feature an explicit 'New Chat' button or icon to clear context like some other chat applications.

The claim that "there isn't a dedicated 'New Chat' button to clear everything away" in Grok's interface is incorrect. Grok, like most chat-based AI tools, provides an option (often a '+' icon or a clear 'New Chat' button) to start a new conversation and clear the previous context.

The description of a 'New Chat' button or icon (like a '+' symbol, speech bubble with a plus, or text 'New Chat'/'Start New Conversation') usually located in the top-left or top-right corner of the Grok chat interface is inaccurate. Grok, as integrated into X, typically does not feature such a prominent, dedicated 'New Chat' button in its main chat view. Users generally start new conversations by simply typing in the input field or navigating back to the Grok section, which initiates a fresh interaction.

Tool is repeatedly called 'Deep Art Effects Pro' throughout the article (subtitle, tags, body), but the actual product by the German company is named simply 'Deep Art Effects' — the 'Pro' suffix appears fabricated/inaccurate as the official product name.

The article attributes specific 'batch processing' capabilities (drop a folder of inputs, apply same style to all, set output folder, hit start) to Deep Art Effects Pro as fact, but these specific batch-processing features cannot be verified as actually existing in the product — reads as content marketing for a tool whose capabilities are not confirmed.

Qwen 3.5 from Alibaba is referenced as a model name; the verified-real list contains "Qwen" and "Alibaba" but "Qwen 3.5" is not confirmed as an official product/version name. This appears to be an invented version number.
Midjourney V8.1 is fabricated — Midjourney's latest major version as of public knowledge is V6/V6.1 (with V7 in alpha at various points), not V8.1. The version number is invented.
Claim that SREFs and Moodboards are 'new-ish' features that V8.1 improves is unverifiable/fabricated as framed — these were introduced around V5/V6, not presented as new in a 'V8.1' release.
Specific UI claim that on midjourney.com the prompt box is 'labelled Imagine' and sits in the 'centre of the screen' cannot be verified for a non-existent V8.1 release.
Claim of a '+ icon on the left side of the prompt box' for image upload on the web interface is unverifiable.

The model name 'Qwen-Image-3.0' appears to be invented or incorrectly versioned. Alibaba's Qwen image model line is 'Qwen-Image' (released August 2025), not 'Qwen-Image-3.0'. No such version exists publicly.

The claim that Qwen-Image-3.0 is available with a 'free Qwen account' at 'chat.qwen.ai' for image generation attributes a specific UI capability to Qwen Chat that is not standard for text-to-image generation in that interface — Qwen Chat is primarily a chat assistant, not documented as a direct image generation portal for this model.
The claim that 'ModelScope at modelscope.cn' lets users 'try different model versions' of Qwen-Image-3.0 implies a specific hosted version that doesn't appear to exist under that name.

Google Meet recordings do not auto-collect into a top-level 'Google Meet' folder in Drive with subfolders per meeting — recordings still land in the host's Drive in the meeting owner's folder with no automatic per-meeting subfolder structure as described.

Google Meet does not have a 'Notes' feature powered by Gemini that 'joins the call as a note taker' — Gemini-powered 'Take notes for me' exists in Google Meet, but the article's description of the menu path (⋮ → Notes) and behavior is not accurately described as a separate folder-drop.

Google Meet captions are not saved as transcript files via the described menu path '⋮ → Captions → Save captions'; transcripts are generated from recorded meetings, not saved manually from a captions menu in this way.

Shortcuts appearing for attendees in their own 'Google Meet' folder is not a real feature — attendees get an email with a link to the recording in the host's Drive, not auto-created Drive shortcuts in a dedicated Meet folder.

The article claims that Midjourney's `/settings` panel contains a 'mode row' with 'pill-shaped buttons labelled Fast, Relax, and sometimes Turbo' — this is fabricated. Midjourney's settings panel does not have this UI; mode toggles are handled differently (e.g., via the /relax and /fast commands or in the web app), and 'Turbo' is not a Midjourney mode.

The article describes a specific web app UI: 'a small text label showing the current mode… usually with a little arrow or dropdown next to it' above/below the Generate button, and suggests looking under 'Job actions' or a three-dot menu — these UI elements are fabricated for Midjourney's web app.

The claim that Relax mode 'typically requires at least a Standard plan or higher' is presented as a specific tier fact without verification and may be wrong (Relax has historically been tied to Standard+ plans, but stating it as a definitive rule without hedging is risky).

The article attributes a specific case study to NTT DATA using "GitHub's Codex" to cut incident analysis time to around 30 minutes. While OpenAI's Codex exists as a legacy product, there is no verified public claim that NTT DATA uses 'GitHub's Codex' (a product not currently marketed under that name by GitHub) in this specific way. This is a fabricated specific claim presented as fact.
GPT-5.6 appears on the verified-real names list but is not mentioned in the article — however, this is not itself a problem. The fabricated 'GitHub's Codex' claim is the real issue.

The article describes a specific voice command 'Alexa, open Conversations' and a panel called 'Conversations' or 'AI Chat' on Echo Show home screens for accessing Alexa+'s language learning mode — these appear to be fabricated UI elements/voice commands. Alexa+'s conversational features are not launched via an 'open Conversations' command or an 'AI Chat' home screen panel.
The article states a specific wake phrase 'Alexa, are you the new Alexa?' to check if Alexa+ is enabled — this does not appear to be a documented Amazon phrase.

The article claims Alexa+ offers a language learning / pronunciation feedback / role-play conversation mode with level selection, which is not a documented feature of Alexa+. Alexa+ is a general AI assistant upgrade; there is no evidence it includes a structured language tutoring mode with beginner/intermediate levels, pronunciation scoring, and role-play scenarios.

The article describes a 'Summarise' button in Mail as a UI element of Apple Intelligence. As of current knowledge, Apple Mail does not have a 'Summarise' button — Apple Intelligence email summarization in Mail works as automatic message summaries that appear at the top of emails in the inbox list, not as a tappable button labeled 'Summarise' that the user must tap.

The article describes a 'Compose' prompt option within Mail's Writing Tools. The Writing Tools panel in Mail offers Rewrite, Proofread, Summary, and tone options (Friendly, Professional, Concise), but the 'Compose' prompt-to-generate feature ('Type a short instruction... then tap the arrow or Send to compose button') is not a documented Mail Writing Tools option — that's a feature in some other contexts, not specifically Mail's Writing Tools panel as described.

The article refers to 'Claude's New Opus Model' as a new top-tier Claude model, but the title attributes a specific model name 'Opus' to a new release without verification. While Claude Opus models exist (e.g., Claude Opus 4.5), describing it as 'new' and tying it to these specific features (long-running agent tasks, professional coding focus) is presented as fact. Claude does have agent capabilities and coding strengths, but the framing as a brand-new release with specific feature attributions needs verification. The specific claims about it being 'new top-of-the-range' and designed specifically for 'long-running agent tasks and professional coding work' are presented as established fact without hedging.

"Claude Opus 5" appears to be an invented or incorrectly named model. Anthropic's naming convention uses the pattern "Claude [version] Opus" (e.g., Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 4 Opus) — the version number precedes the variant name, not the other way around. No "Claude Opus 5" matches Anthropic's established naming scheme or is known to exist; the model name in the title and body is fabricated or wrong.

Midjourney V8.2: this version number is not verified and is likely fabricated. Midjourney's current versioning uses numeric releases (V5, V5.1, V5.2, V6, V6.1, V7) as of the article context, not 'V8.2'. The article presents V8.2 features (widened aesthetic range, reduced failure rate, smarter personalisation) as established facts of a specific update that does not appear to exist.

Midjourney does not have a documented '--style' parameter as described. The known parameters include --stylize (--s), --style (in limited form for Niji), but the article's specific framing and examples ('more editorial, more cinematic, or more photographic') as style values are not an accurate representation of how the --style parameter works in Midjourney.

The tool 'Cohere Transcribe Arabic' is invented — Cohere does not have a product called 'Cohere Transcribe Arabic' or a transcription feature specifically branded for Arabic on their dashboard. The article describes specific UI flows (dialect picker, upload, transcribe button) attributed to Cohere that do not exist in this form.

Invented model name: 'Qwen3.6-35B-A3B' does not appear to exist. Qwen's known open coding models include Qwen2.5-Coder (in various sizes) and Qwen3-Coder. The 'Qwen3.6-35B-A3B' naming is fabricated and is repeated multiple times throughout the article as if it were a real, recently released model.

Possibly wrong Ollama model tag: the article suggests `ollama run qwen2.5-coder:1.5b` as a smaller alternative, which should be verified. The base `qwen2.5-coder` tag on Ollama may not exist exactly as written (actual variants are typically size-suffixed like 1.5b, 7b, etc.). This is borderline — flagging as low-confidence.

The article states the Gemini app icon is 'a four-pointed star in blue, pink and white' — Gemini's app icon is a four-pointed spark/star shape, but it is described as blue and white (gradient blue), not 'blue, pink and white'. This appears to be an invented detail.

The article mentions specific UI elements like a 'waveform icon' near the bottom-right for Gemini Live with specific button placement ('waveform icon or a Live button near the bottom-right') — Gemini Live exists but the exact icon description and placement may be fabricated.

The article references paid plans 'Google AI Pro / Advanced' as plan names without verification — these plan names may not exactly match Google's current offerings (e.g., Google AI Plus, Google AI Pro exists but 'Advanced' is unclear).

Article claims Google launched three specific new models: 'Gemini 3.6 Flash', '3.5 Flash-Lite', and '3.5 Flash Cyber' — these appear to be fabricated model names. Google's real Gemini family naming uses versions like Gemini 1.5 Flash, 2.0 Flash, 2.5 Flash, with 'Flash-Lite' as a real suffix, but '3.5 Flash Cyber' and 'Gemini 3.6 Flash' as described do not correspond to known real product names and the 'Cyber' cybersecurity-tuned variant appears invented.

The article presents 'Take notes for me' capturing visual screenshots of slides/charts and embedding them into a Google Doc as an upcoming feature. I cannot verify that Google has officially announced this specific visual-screenshot functionality for Google Meet's 'Take notes for me' feature. This appears to be a fabricated feature/announcement rather than a verified news report.

Specific implementation details are stated as fact (e.g., screenshots placed 'right next to the relevant summary line', a Google Doc saved to organizer's Drive with screenshots, a copy emailed to participants, a new Workspace admin setting to toggle the visual screenshot feature) without sourcing — these read as invented specifics rather than reported facts.

The product is named 'Personal Computer' and described as Perplexity's AI-powered browser for Windows. Perplexity's actual AI browser is called 'Comet' — 'Personal Computer' is not a real product name from Perplexity. The entire article describes a fabricated product.
The article claims the browser 'costs nothing to download' — Perplexity Comet has a paid tier (Comet Plus) and Pro features, so stating it is free as fact is a fabricated pricing claim.

The article states Perplexity's AI browser is 'now on Windows' — Perplexity Comet launched on Windows in 2024/2025, which is broadly consistent, but combined with the wrong product name this likely misrepresents the actual launch details.

The example prompt in Step 1 contains Chinese characters '海洋' mixed into an otherwise English sentence, which is a clear formatting/translation error that appears fabricated or corrupted rather than intentional content.

The 'Help me create' button as described — a floating button in the bottom-right of a new Google Form that opens a side panel for describing a quiz, with a 'paperclip' icon for attaching Drive files (Docs, Slides, PDFs) as source materials, and that drafts questions with marked correct answers — does not match the known functionality of Gemini in Google Forms. As of current knowledge, Gemini in Google Forms (the 'Help me create' feature) does not support attaching source documents from Drive to ground quiz generation, and the described paperclip/file-attach workflow within the panel is not a documented feature.

The claim that the source-attachment feature is 'one of the most useful bits' allowing Gemini to base questions on an uploaded Google Doc/Slide/PDF appears to be fabricated, as this capability is not a verified part of the Gemini-in-Google Forms feature.

The specific UI element descriptions (floating 'Help me create' button in bottom-right, side panel with 'Generate'/'Insert' button, paperclip icon inside the panel, 'Draft ready' message) are presented as definitive product UI but cannot be verified and read as invented specifics rather than honest hedged guidance.
GPT-Realtime is not a verified model name — OpenAI's real-time voice API product is 'Realtime API' (or 'gpt-4o-realtime-preview' model). 'GPT-Realtime' as a model name appears fabricated.

The article claims Gmail has rolled out a warning when hitting Reply All on a thread where you were BCC'd, but no such feature is documented in any official Google release notes or Workspace updates. This is a fabricated product feature attributed to Gmail.
